newsitem.title: KENYA: Sudan said to clear way for talks to end civil war.
newsitem.headline: Sudan said to clear way for talks to end civil war.

text.p: African leaders said on Wednesday Sudan accepted a framework for negotiations to end its 14-year civil war -- clearing the way for a resumption of talks.

"The summit welcomed the acceptance by the government of Sudan of the declaration of principles as the basis for discussions and negotiations," the five leaders said in a statement at the end of their two-day summit on Sudan.
"The summit considered this development a major breakthrough in the peace initiative," said the five African leaders, including Sudanese President Lieutenant-General Omar Hassan al-Bashir.

"This will enable the parties to the conflict to freely discuss and negotiate on all the points enshrined in the declaration of principles," they added in the statement read out at State House in Nairobi by Kenya's foreign minister.
Peace talks in Nairobi between Bashir and Sudanese rebel leader John Garang mediated by regional states broke down in September 1994 when Sudan refused to sign the declaration of principles.

Sudan's Islamist-backed government had objected to the declaration saying religion and the state were separate and endorsing self-determination for southern Sudan, wrecked by civil war between rebels and government forces since 1983.

Khartoum accepted the principle of self-determination when it signed peace agreements with several southern groups in April but not the largest rebel movement -- Garang's Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA).
The summit was organised as part of a peace initiative by the Inter-Governmental Authority on Development (IGAD).
"The summit requests the chairman of the IGAD peace initiative to take the necessary measures aimed at a speedy resumption of the negotiations," the African leaders said.

"The summit called on the parties to the conflict to create the conducive environment necessary for the resumption of negotiations," said the leaders and a representative of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, who failed to attend the summit.
The Nairobi summit however made little progress on the problem of the civil war in Somalia, which was also discussed.
"The summit noted with grave concern that peace in Somalia remains elusive," said the leaders.
The summit was hosted by Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi, Eritrean President Isayas Afewerki and Djibouti President Hassan Gouled Aptidon also attended the summit, which started on Tuesday.

A diplomat told Reuters Museveni failed to attend the summit because he demanded Sudan first press for the release of 21 schoolgirls abducted in October in northern Uganda by Ugandan rebels with bases in south Sudan.
The schoolgirls were abducted by the Lord's Resistance Army, which Uganda says is backed and armed by Sudan's government.
